title: Bartonellosis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Bartonellosis encompasses a group of emerging zoonotic infections caused by Bartonella species, fastidious, gram-negative, facultative, intracellular bacteria that infect red blood cells and endothelial cells, often causing prolonged bacteremia in humans and animals. Over 45 Bartonella species have been identified, with 12 linked to human disease. Clinically significant species include Bartonella henselae , Bartonella quintana , and Bartonella bacilliformis . B henselae causes cat-scratch disease, culture-negative endocarditis, and bacillary peliosis hepatis. B quintana , historically associated with trench fever, also causes chronic bacteremia, bacillary angiomatosis, and subacute endocarditis, particularly in individuals living in crowded or unhygienic conditions. B bacilliformis , endemic to South America, causes Carrion disease, presenting as acute Oroya fever with high mortality if untreated, followed by verruga peruana. Bartonellosis is often underrecognized due to nonspecific clinical presentations.

title: Bartonellosis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course equips participants to recognize bartonellosis, interpret clinical and laboratory findings, and apply species-specific antimicrobial strategies. Clinicians identify at-risk individuals and initiate evaluation, microbiologists confirm diagnoses, pharmacists guide antimicrobial selection, and nurses monitor adherence and response. Interprofessional collaboration is highlighted, which enhances early detection, optimized management, and improved survival and quality of life for patients with this disease.

title: Bartonellosis -- Introduction
content: Bartonella spp are intracellular, facultative, gram-negative bacteria that cause zoonotic infections in humans globally. Bartonella is an emerging and expanding genus, currently reported to have over 45 species, 12 of which are associated with human infections. [1] . The species most commonly associated with bartonellosis in humans are B henselae, B quintana and B bacilliformis . B henselae causes cat-scratch disease, and other clinical syndromes, such as culture-negative endocarditis and bacillary peliosis hepatis. [2] B quintana , a louse-borne infection that was historically the cause of trench fever, is a neglected cause of syndromes, such as acute febrile illness, chronic bacteremia, bacillary angiomatosis, and subacute endocarditis. [3] Transmission of B quintana is by infected body lice, and risk factors include living in crowded, unhygienic conditions as well as experiencing homelessness. [1] [4] [5]

title: Bartonellosis -- Introduction
content: Recent reports have documented transmission of B quintana through organ transplantation from deceased persons who experienced homelessness. [4] [6] B bacilliformis is endemic to the South American Andean valleys and causes Carrion disease. [7] [8] B bacilliformis is transmitted to humans via the bite of the sandfly Lutzomyia verrucarum. Carrion disease presents in 2 clinical forms: The acute phase of Oroya fever is a severe, febrile, hemolytic illness with untreated mortality rates reaching up to 80% to 90%. [7] [8] The chronic phase, known as verruga peruana, typically appears weeks to months later as indolent and disfiguring angioproliferative skin lesions, which are rarely life-threatening.

title: Bartonellosis -- Etiology
content: Bartonellae are considered an emerging and expanding genus, with more than 45 Bartonella species currently described, at least 12 of which have been associated with human infections. [1] Bartonella spp are gram-negative, facultative intracellular bacteria transmitted to humans through arthropod vectors or direct contact with animals. B henselae is responsible for cat-scratch disease, a zoonotic disease typically presenting with regional lymphadenitis. [2] B quintana , historically recognized as the agent of trench fever, is transmitted by the human body louse and may also manifest as endocarditis or bacillary angiomatosis, particularly in immunocompromised hosts. [1] [3] [4] [5] In contrast, B bacilliformis , restricted to Andean regions and transmitted by sand flies, produces Carrion disease, characterized by a biphasic course, with acute Oroya fever followed by a chronic angioproliferative cutaneous eruption known as verruga peruana. [7] [8]

title: Bartonellosis -- Epidemiology
content: Bartonella spp are intracellular, facultative, gram-negative, slow-growing bacteria that cause zoonotic infections in humans globally. Bartonella is an emerging and expanding genus, currently comprising over 45 different species, 12 of which are associated with human diseases. [1] These Bartonella species include: B henselae, B quintana, B bacilliformis, B elizabethae, B grahamii, B clarridgeiae, B koehlerae, B vinsonii ( especially subspecies B berkhoffii and B arupensis), B washoensis, B rochalimae, B melophagi, B alsatica, and B tamiae ( see Table 1 below). [10]

title: Bartonellosis -- Epidemiology
content: Bartonella exemplifies the advantages of integrated approaches: Bartonella spp infect various animal hosts, are increasingly recognized as causative agents of human disease, and are transmitted by arthropod vectors, such as fleas, lice, and sand flies. Bartonellosis is characterized by long-lasting erythrocyte-associated bacteremia across multiple reservoir hosts. [11] Advances in molecular epidemiology have highlighted the extensive diversity within the genus Bartonella . Over time, multiple species have been identified, each exhibiting host specificity to different mammalian reservoirs and relying on distinct arthropod vectors for transmission. [11] These infections appear globally distributed and affect a wide range of species. At least 13 Bartonella species are currently considered pathogenic to humans, with B bacilliformis , B quintana , and B henselae accounting for most clinically significant cases. [11]

title: Bartonellosis -- Epidemiology
content: Bartonella infections are often persistent and asymptomatic in their natural reservoir hosts. These bacteria can infect various cell types, including erythrocytes, endothelial cells, human stem cells, and macrophages. [12] Erythrocyte invasion is specific to the host and is mediated by the Trw type IV secretion system, which promotes selective adhesion to erythrocytes. [12] Both reservoir and incidental hosts can develop localized tissue lesions, and bacterial replication within vascular tissues may lead to angioproliferative growths and inflammation. [13]

title: Bartonellosis -- Epidemiology
content: Evidence suggests that ticks, red ants, and spiders may transmit Bartonella . [14] Bed bugs have been implicated in the transmission cycle of B quintana and have been artificially infected. [15] The diversity of newly discovered Bartonella species, the large number and ecologically diverse animal reservoir hosts, and the large spectrum of arthropod vectors that can transmit these bacteria among animals and humans are significant causes for public health concern. title: Bartonellosis -- Epidemiology
content: Cats and the cat flea, Ctenocephalides felis, act as vectors for transmission of cat scratch disease. [16] Study results have confirmed that the flea transmits the pathogen, which is critical for sustaining the circulation of B henselae within the feline population. Transmission occurs when flea feces containing the bacteria contaminate feeding sites, scratches, or bite wounds, enabling spread between cats and from cats to humans. [17] Within the flea, B henselae replicates in the intestinal tract and is continuously shed in the feces over the insect’s approximately 12-day lifespan

title: Bartonellosis -- Epidemiology
content: Many cats harbor Bartonella infections without exhibiting overt clinical symptoms, although they may undergo intermittent bacteremia that lasts for prolonged periods. Concurrent infection with multiple Bartonella species is frequently observed. More recent research has shown that other arthropod vectors, including ticks, lice, chiggers, and mosquitoes, are likely also implicated in the spread of the disease among humans. [10] [18] Bartonella spp infection in cats has been reported as endemic in many countries, and studies in humans have found variable seroprevalence rates. [19] The global incidence of cat-scratch disease was reported to be 6.4 cases per 100,000 in adults and 9.4 cases per 100,000 in children aged 5 to 9 years, respectively. The highest incidence is reported in the southeastern United States, peaking in January, late summer, and fall. [20] B quintana

title: Bartonellosis -- Epidemiology
content: B quintan a is a bacterium restricted to human hosts and louse vectors. Epidemic and sporadic outbreaks of trench fever have been reported globally since the early 20th century, with the most significant epidemics occurring during World Wars I and II. [5] Trench fever, the earliest recognized disease caused by Bartonella quintana , is estimated to have affected more than one million individuals during World War I. [5] The human body louse, Pediculus humanus, is the predominant vector responsible for the transmission of trench fever caused by B artonella quintana . [5] Bartonellosis with B quintana is now a reemerging infection, transmitted by the human body louse in conditions of poverty, overcrowding, and in persons who experience homelessness. [21] Transmission of B quintana has also been reported through organ transplantation from harvested organs, mostly from high-risk populations. [6] Clinical manifestations include trench fever, culture-negative endocarditis, chronic bacteremia, and bacillary angiomatosis, a proliferative vascular disease seen in immunocompetent, but primarily immunocompromised patients. [3] [5]

title: Bartonellosis -- Epidemiology
content: Carrion disease is caused by Bartonella bacilliformis, w hich is endemic to Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador; sporadic cases have been reported in Chile, Guatemala, and Bolivia. [8] The transmission of Bartonella bacilliformis occurs via the bite of the female sandfly Lutzomyia. Infections with B. bacilliformis are characterized by two distinct clinical forms: Oroya fever, an acute febrile bacteremia characterized by fever and hemolytic anemia, which carries a mortality rate up to 90% if left untreated. Verruga Peruana is a chronic, eruptive cutaneous disease that can emerge weeks and months after the acute phase. [8]

title: Bartonellosis -- Pathophysiology
content: Once inside the host, Bartonella spp primarily target CD34+ progenitor cells, which are precursors of endothelial cells that line blood vessels and tissues. Following entry, the bacterium inhibits programmed cell death and establishes a protective vacuole that shelters it from host defenses. [12] [22] A key virulence factor is lipid A, an endotoxin present in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria. [12] [22] The capacity of Bartonella to invade both erythrocytes and endothelial cells is central to its pathogenesis. By modulating immune responses, the pathogen increases host vulnerability to secondary bacterial infections. [12] [22] After the initial acute phase, Bartonella disseminates into the endovascular, lymphatic, and other organ systems, resulting in a wide range of clinical manifestations.

title: Bartonellosis -- History and Physical
content: A comprehensive personal, travel, and social history should be obtained, and a physical examination should be performed in any patient seeking medical attention. In cases of suspected cat scratch disease, the clinical history may be vague or poorly reported, as the initial inoculation is often unnoticed. The differential diagnosis for each syndrome can be extensive, and diagnosis may be delayed due to the need for a comprehensive workup and the fact that Bartonella infection is often not initially considered. title: Bartonellosis -- History and Physical
content: Cat scratch disease (CSD) is transmitted by a bite, lick, or scratch of open skin by an infected cat. Cutaneous manifestations typically begin within 1 to 10 days of exposure and progress through vesicular, erythematous, and papular phases. [23] Regional lymphadenopathy typically appears 1 to 3 weeks after inoculation; fever is often reported. CSD is usually benign and self-limiting. Disseminated CSD with granulomatous involvement of visceral organs, eyes, and bones can occur, but this is rare. [24] [25]

title: Bartonellosis -- History and Physical
content: Infective neuroretinitis : After the lymphatic system, the eye is the most frequently affected organ; 5% to 10% of CSD cases present with ocular manifestations. [23] [26] Ocular involvement can be subclinical, and visual symptoms may not be a common presenting complaint. Neuroretinitis is an optic neuropathy classically characterized by optic disc swelling in the presence of a partial or complete macular star. [23] [27]

content: Neurological manifestations reported in patients diagnosed with cat scratch disease include encephalopathy, transverse myelitis, radiculitis, and cerebellar ataxia. [29]

title: Bartonellosis -- History and Physical
content: Culture-negative endocarditis. Another presentation of infection includes negative culture endocarditis. Although several species have been implicated in causing endocarditis, B henselae and Bartonella quintana account for approximately 95% of endocarditis cases caused by Bartonella . [30]

title: Bartonellosis -- History and Physical
content: Severe, progressive, disseminated disease may occur in immunocompromised individuals, especially those with HIV infection and organ transplants. Without therapy, the infection spreads systemically and can involve virtually any organ, and the outcome is sometimes fatal.

title: Bartonellosis -- History and Physical
content: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferative disorder that affects immunocompromised individuals, especially in those with HIV/AIDS. [31] BA is caused by either B henselae or B quintana and is characterized by cutaneous lesions, subcutaneous masses, spleen, liver, and bone lesions. This is a vascular proliferative disease that most often involves the skin, but may also affect other organs. The clinical differential diagnosis includes pyogenic granuloma, hemangioma, subcutaneous tumors, and Kaposi sarcoma. The skin lesions are very similar to those reported for verruga peruana, the chronic form of Carrion's disease. Lesions can also involve the bone marrow, liver, spleen, or lymph nodes.

title: Bartonellosis -- History and Physical
content: Peliosis hepatis (PH) is a vascular proliferation of sinusoidal hepatic capillaries resulting in blood-filled spaces in the liver. [2] This disease was first described in patients with tuberculosis and advanced cancers and correlated with the use of drugs such as anabolic steroids. B henselae is now recognized as an infectious cause of PH in HIV-infected patients. [32] PH has also been reported in organ transplant recipients and can occur simultaneously with splenic peliosis and bacillary angiomatosis of the skin in HIV-infected individuals.

content: Trench fever, caused by Bartonella quintana, presents clinical features including malaise, fever, headache, bone pain, and splenomegaly. The pattern of fever associated with trench fever is highly variable, ranging from a single episode to a persistent fever lasting several days. [33] Bartonella bacilliformis

title: Bartonellosis -- History and Physical
content: The clinical manifestations of infection caused by B bacilliformis include an acute phase, Oroya fever, characterized by fever, malaise, headache, intraerythrocytic anemia, tachycardia, and hepatomegaly, and a chronic phase (verruga peruana), characterized by endothelial cell-derived, blood-filled tumors erupting cutaneously, which appear approximately 2 to 8 weeks after the acute phase. [7] [34] [35] Chronic Bartonella infection can be associated with relapsing low-grade fever. [35] Chronic eye problems include blurred vision, photophobia, and eye irritation. Bartonella commonly infects the bone marrow, resulting in bone pain, most commonly in the tibia. Anemia can occur from Bartonella scavenging nutrients from red blood cells. Neurological symptoms include poor balance, decreased cognition, memory impairment, insomnia, and restlessness. [7] [35]

Neurological symptoms include poor balance, decreased cognition, memory impairment, insomnia, and restlessness. [7] [35]

title: Bartonellosis -- Evaluation
content: The diagnosis of CSD requires a multifaceted approach that integrates clinical presentation with molecular, serological, and histopathological findings. The diagnostic modalities commonly used to diagnose Bartonella infection include: serological testing, culture, histopathology, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

title: Bartonellosis -- Evaluation -- Serology
content: Serology remains the most cost-effective initial diagnostic test. Indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays can detect antibodies against B henselae . IFA was the first microbiological test available for CSD; however, its positive predictive value is variable, especially during the early stages of the disease. In some studies' results, the positive predictive value of IFA reached 91.4%, whereas other results reported lower sensitivity. Typical sensitivity of Bartonella henselae immunoglobulin (Ig) G and M serology ranges from approximately 50% to 80%, with specificity generally high at 90% to 100%. [36] Sensitivity increases when clinical suspicion for CSD is high. An IgM titer of 1:16 or greater indicates an acute infection, which is detectable for up to 3 months in approximately 50% of patients. [37] An IgG titer of 1:256 or greater is evidence of current or past infection. Unlike culture and PCR, serology does not rely on the presence of bacteria in the blood and can also be used to monitor response to therapy, even though titers may persist for years. A drawback of serological testing is that cross-reactions occur between antibodies for B henselae and B quintana and with both Chlamydia species and Coxiella burnetii, which may limit interpretation. Furthermore, serological tests do not differentiate between Bartonella species.

title: Bartonellosis -- Evaluation -- Culture
content: The culture of Bartonella species provides a definitive diagnosis, but it is time-consuming, expensive, and technically challenging. Bartonella spp are slow-growing and fastidious, with primary isolation often requiring 1 to 4 weeks of incubation on blood agar plates and, in some cases, up to 21 days. [38] Due to these limitations, culture is not routinely recommended in clinical practice.

title: Bartonellosis -- Evaluation -- Visualization by special stains.
content: Histopathological examination of the affected tissue typically reveals neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltration, along with scattered cellular debris. Warthin-Starry silver staining can reveal small, darkly staining bacteria, while electron microscopy demonstrates pleomorphic bacilli with a trilaminar cell wall. For B bacilliformis , Giemsa staining highlights cytoplasmic inclusions known as Rocha-Lima inclusions. [39]

title: Bartonellosis -- Evaluation -- Polymerase chain reaction
content: PCR assays can be used to detect DNA from tissue samples, such as lymph nodes or other clinical specimens, eg, blood, to detect Bartonella DNA. PCR offers high specificity and rapid identification; however, its sensitivity varies, ranging from 30% to 76% depending on the sample type, species, and disease stage. When tested on blood and culture samples, a study by Choat et al reported a real-time PCR test targeting the vomp region of B quintana with 100% sensitivity and specificity. [40]

title: Bartonellosis -- Treatment / Management
content: Bartonella species demonstrate susceptibility to numerous antibiotics when grown in culture, including penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, chloramphenicol, tetracyclines, macrolides, rifampin, fluoroquinolones, and co-trimoxazole. Nonetheless, in vitro activity does not reliably predict in vivo effectiveness. For instance, despite exhibiting a very low minimum inhibitory concentration in vitro, penicillin has proven ineffective in clinical settings. [41]

title: Bartonellosis -- Treatment / Management
content: Management of cat scratch disease depends on the clinical presentation of the disease. Patients presenting with mild symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy and fever, should be offered supportive care, as the disease is usually self-limiting and antimicrobial therapy is not necessary. [42] However, study results have shown that using a single antimicrobial regimen will significantly reduce the duration and size of the lymphadenopathy. The antimicrobial agents that can be used include erythromycin, doxycycline, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, and rifampin. Depending on the disease and pathogen, these agents can be used in various combinations and for different durations of therapy:

title: Bartonellosis -- Differential Diagnosis
content: B henselae can cause CSD, which most commonly presents as lymphadenitis. The differential diagnosis of CSD: Mycobacterial infections (tuberculous or atypical mycobacteria) Toxoplasmosis Viral lymphadenitis (EBV, CMV, HIV) Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes lymphadenitis Tularemia Lymphoma or leukemia Coccidioidomycosis and valley fever Leishmaniosis Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) Nocardiosis Sarcoidosis Sporotrichosis Syphilis Toxoplasmosis

title: Bartonellosis -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Prevention of Bartonella infections involves simple measures tailored to the specific mode of transmission: Cat scratch disease: Reducing transmission from cats can be achieved by providing proper care for pets, avoiding scratches or bites, keeping cats indoors whenever possible, regularly treating cats to eliminate fleas, and washing hands thoroughly after handling cats. Trench fever: Preventing infection requires minimizing exposure to human body lice and promptly treating infestations if they occur. Carrion disease ( B bacilliformis ): Prevention focuses on avoiding bites from infected sandflies. Protective measures include wearing clothing with long sleeves, using insect repellents, and sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets in areas where B bacilliiformis is endemic. These preventive strategies, along with public education about vectors and risk factors, are crucial in reducing the incidence of Bartonella -related diseases.

title: Bartonellosis -- Pearls and Other Issues -- Ongoing Research
content: Findings suggest that Bartonella spp can be used to induce angiogenesis, which could potentially be utilized to circumvent blocked arteries in the heart, promote the formation of new blood vessels in damaged limbs, and accelerate wound healing in damaged tissues. Current investigations are focused on understanding the genetic basis of the mechanisms that are involved in the causation of angiogenesis. [48]

title: Bartonellosis -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The diagnosis and management of CSD are best approached by an interprofessional team, including an infectious disease consultant, emergency department physician, internal medicine physician and nursing staff. Management depends largely on the clinical presentation. Patients with mild disease, such as localized lymphadenopathy and low-grade fever, often do not require antimicrobial therapy due to the self-limiting nature of CSD. [42] Supportive care, including pain management and monitoring, is typically sufficient for these cases.
